semantics.note: Leaving out the rhetorical 'most-prominent hypesters' is fine. The proposition keeps both parts: millions spent on marketing, and a product that doesn't exist as sold. Identifying it as Agentforce fits the context.

contract.note: Reading 'millions' as at least $2M, and the capability point as a material mismatch rather than total nonexistence, is a fair, ordinary reading. Requiring both parts matches the sentence.

evidence.note: The Bloomberg reporter's own summary, dated 2026-05-22. It says some promoted functionality was months or years from deployment, and Benioff calls it forward-looking vision. It has no spending figure and doesn't show how the demos were represented, so it can't settle the claim.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no Agentforce-specific spending figure, so the 'millions' part can't be checked. Ford's post partly backs a gap between what was promoted and what was deployed. But it doesn't reproduce the demos or their disclaimers, and Benioff says they were presented as future vision. Neither part is settled, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the original wording, including the claims about intent ('intentionally', 'deliberately'). It is an observation that mixes in claims about motive.

contract.note: Splitting the claim into three parts (fees were reduced, coverage knowingly left this out, Musk's motive was publicity) is fair. Treating 'those covering' as broad coverage is the ordinary reading. The intent parts need direct evidence that would rarely be available.

evidence.note: Reuters coverage of the expected Q2 profit explicitly reports that, per SpaceX's filing, fees would be reduced during the May–June ramp-up. This contradicts the blanket claim that coverage ignored the reduction. It does confirm that reduced fees existed. It shows nothing about anyone's motive.
The TechCrunch profitability brief doesn't mention the fee reduction. Leaving it out doesn't show the omission was knowing or deliberate.

reviews.rationale: Holds: reduced May–June fees existed, as reported from the SpaceX filing. Contradicted: the blanket claim that coverage ignored them, since Reuters reported the reduction in the same story as the profit expectation. Unresolved: whether journalists knowingly concealed it and whether Musk meant to engineer a headline. No direct evidence of motive, and Reuters describes the reduction as tied to a capacity ramp.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Keeps the metric (non-GAAP operating margin), the quarter, the figure, and the separate claim that ChatGPT growth has stalled.

contract.note: Reading 'ChatGPT growth' as active users, checked through April, is a reasonable reading an informed reader would take, though it is the evaluator's choice. The two parts are tested separately, which is appropriate.

evidence.note: PYMNTS cites The Information: OpenAI told investors its adjusted operating margin was -122% in Q1 2026. That matches the basis and the period. Its user figures (about 920M weekly users in February, 905M Q1 average) suggest softer usage but don't establish a plateau through April.
Repeats the -122% figure from the same source, so it isn't independent. The 905M quarterly average missing a target doesn't show growth stalled through April.

reviews.rationale: The margin part holds: reputable reporting on investor disclosures gives a -122% adjusted operating margin for Q1 2026. The growth part is unresolved: the packet has no consistent active-user series through April. A February peak above the Q1 average hints at softness but doesn't establish a sustained plateau.

semantics.note: 'I believe' states an unqualified expectation, not a graded hedge, so this is a scorable forecast. The proposition keeps 'vast majority' and 'unused and/or unfinished'. The second clause about startups dying once VC money dries up is left out; it is a separate conditional and should be its own claim.

contract.note: Fixing the group of projects at publication, counting projects, and treating 'go unused' as the final outcome are all fair readings. The contract labels the claim 'retrospective', which is a minor labeling slip and doesn't affect the result.

evidence.note: CBRE's H1 2026 report shows low vacancy and high preleasing in eight North American markets. That is contrary context, but it measures leasing, not the final outcome for the AI projects in this claim.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline, and no lasting outcomes (completion and real use, or permanent abandonment) are recorded for the fixed group of projects. CBRE's low vacancy figures are contrary context but don't meet the early-resolution rule. Not scored yet.
